beats.label: SHAPED BY

cue.prompt: The system taught you how to move.

slides.title: BERLIN IS YELLOW
beats: Berlin 1925: "totally black and white." The weather, the people, everything.
Reunification 1990: five or six colors, "most of them were beige."
"Beige is you have a room of people that decide the color is beige. Which means it's no color."
"So I made everything yellow. And they will never ever change that. Because they can't anymore."
slides.note:
→ "This is Spiekermann on stage, decades later, telling the triumph version."

→ "Beige is the villain here — it's the negotiation table rendered as a color. The absence of a choice, presented as a choice."

→ "One person, one decision, applied across the whole system: yellow buses, yellow trams, yellow U-Bahn."

→ "And then it escapes him — the choice becomes infrastructure that constrains every designer who comes after."

slides.text: Two versions. Both true.
slides.note: → "But there's another version of this story."\n\n→ "Eye magazine, 1995, three years after handoff: 'almost no control over how the work has been used... asked whether it worked, nobody knows.'"

slides.text: You won't perceive the effect.
slides.note:
→ "His actual line, from a different project: 'One of the best things about designing type is that you know that they don't. You won't perceive the effect.'"

→ "That lands directly on what Clynes & Kline will call 'unconsciously' — if you notice your prosthesis constantly, integration has failed."

⚑ Do NOT use fabricated 'disappears into use' quote from earlier drafts. This is his real words.

slides.text: The gap between them is the condition of designing infrastructure at all.
slides.note: → "On stage: triumph. In print: loss of control. Both Spiekermann. Both true."\n\n→ "He shaped the city, and the institution shaped him right back. That gap is the beat — don't resolve it."

slides.alt: Yellow Berlin bus on city street
slides.note: → "This is what 'they will never ever change that' looks like."\n\n→ "Every yellow bus, every yellow tram — carrying forward one designer's choice from 1992."

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 6 min · the brief's "public transit and cities" beat, and my credential — I've met him and published on him

⚑ Do NOT say he designed the U-Bahn map · no ridership/legibility numbers · no MetaDesign co-founder names · never repeat the Green Party claim

beats.label: RESHAPED BY

slides.title: THE PEOPLE'S SIDEWALKS
beats: "We've tried cripples before, and they just don't work out."
Berkeley builds curb ramps. The disabled community says: wrong.
Flat ramps erase the edge blind pedestrians navigate by.
So they mapped 125 of them and drew the compromise themselves.
slides.note:
→ "Ed Roberts got polio at fourteen. Berkeley admitted him in 1962, and a dean's recorded reaction was 'we've tried cripples before, and they just don't work out.'"

→ "The only building that could hold his 800-pound iron lung was the campus hospital. He took it — on condition it be treated as a dorm, not a medical facility."

→ "More disabled students arrive. They name themselves the Rolling Quads, and start using civil-rights language for something that had always been framed as charity."

→ "1969, after the People's Park riots, Berkeley renovates Telegraph Avenue and puts in wide flat curb ramps."

→ "The response is not gratitude. Flat ramps erase the edge blind pedestrians navigate by, and the diagonal angle pushes wheelchairs toward turning cars."

→ "And here's the best detail — the disabled community was split against itself. Wheelchair users and blind pedestrians wanted opposite things."

→ "So from 1970 to 1974 they map 125 curb-cut locations along Telegraph and Shattuck, and propose a steeper cut set outside the crossing. A compromise they negotiated among themselves."

slides.alt: Ed Roberts in iron lung at UC Berkeley
slides.note: → "Ed Roberts — 800-pound iron lung, campus hospital room, on condition it be treated as a dorm."\n\n→ "The person who changed how we move through cities. And the machine that kept him alive while he did it."

slides.text: Everyone with a stroller uses what they won.
slides.note:
→ "First planned wheelchair-accessible route in the United States, designed by disabled people."

→ "Sixteen years later the ADA makes it federal law. Today every stroller, suitcase and hand truck rides it."

→ "That's the loop closing: the system defined them as unable to move, they moved anyway, they redrew the environment — and the redrawn environment redefined everyone else's mobility."

slides.text: The geometry was fought over. The texture was a gift.
slides.note:
→ "One more detail, because it's the whole talk in miniature."

→ "The ramp's geometry — that was fought over in public, in Berkeley, by a community split against itself."

→ "But the bumpy yellow texture on it has the opposite origin. Truncated domes — tenji paving — invented in 1965 by one Japanese engineer, Seiichi Miyake, for one friend who was losing his sight. First laid in Okayama in 1967, and it spread across the world from there."

→ "Two completely different politics — one collective and contested, one singular and quiet — and you're standing on both at once."

· Miyake is the SETUP for the language bridge next. Don't rush off it.

slides.alt: Fresh curb cut with yellow tactile warning surface - raised yellow domes embedded in concrete ramp
slides.note:
→ "This is what they're both standing on. Fresh concrete, yellow tenji, compromise geometry."

→ "Berkeley politics made the ramp. Miyake's gift made the surface. Same infrastructure, two completely different origins."

→ "Adapt, resist, reshape — and then it inherits."

· Read as a sequence, not options. Berkeley ran all four.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 6 min · the brief's "adapt, resist, reshape" promise · Miyake sets up the language bridge, don't drop it

⚑ Roberts did NOT found the Center for Independent Living — say he led it or guided its growth · Berkeley did NOT invent the curb cut (Kalamazoo, 1940s, disabled veterans) · defensible claim is first PLANNED accessible route, designed by disabled people · Miyake: 1965 invented, 1967 first installed Okayama

· Sources: Williamson, "The People's Sidewalks," Boom Spring 2012 · Miyake: adatile.com, V&A, Reliance Foundry

beats.label: THE BRIDGE

cue.prompt: Every word in your mouth was built by someone else.

slides.text: You didn't design either one. You move through both.
slides.note:
→ "The curb you cross was fought over by people you'll never meet."

→ "The pad you cross it on was invented across the world, for one person, decades ago."

→ "You didn't design either — you didn't even fight over them — and you move through both without a thought."

slides.text: Every word in your mouth was built by someone else.
slides.note:
→ "Now scale that up. Every word in your mouth was built by someone else too."

→ "Some of it fought over, some of it a quiet gift from one person to another. None of it yours alone."

→ "Which answers the question I planted at the start: did you invent the words? No. And it was never really about AI — it's been true all along."

· Language is the oldest prosthesis. This is the keystone — the whole back half rests here.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 2 min · the pivot from infrastructure to language · curb = collective/contested authorship, pad = inherited/singular authorship — both feed the resolution

⚑ This is the callback to the opener. Say 'did you invent the words' out loud so the loop is audible.

beats.label: RESPONSIBILITY

cue.prompt: For whose interests does the interface serve?

slides.title: REGENT / THE SEAGLIDER
beats: Brief: an interface for a captain who can fly.
Then the test pilot showed up. Call sign: Bob Dylan.
"That's not where I expect it to be."
We weren't designing interface. We were translating fluency.
slides.note:
→ "Regent builds a ground-effect craft that skims above the water."

→ "The client defined the operator as a mariner. One wheel, one throttle — a captain that can fly."

→ "But the operational scope was aviation-grade and the mental model was maritime. That gap was the entire design problem."

→ "Then a test pilot joins. Ex-Air Force, F-16s in service, 747s commercially, tens of thousands of hours. Call sign a folksinger's name — we called him Bob Dylan."

→ "He liked every concept. Every concept was wrong."

→ "Not messy, not unpolished — they didn't match the logic his body had spent decades building. He'd tell me what he couldn't see, not because it was missing from the UI but because it wasn't where his body expected it."

→ "The real user changed, and the entire prompt changed with it."

· Name the table: me, business development, product management, the CTO, program directors — all genuinely good people. Then the pilot arrived and reordered everything.

slides.alt: Regent seaglider flying above water surface
slides.note: → "A ground-effect craft that skims above the water. Not quite ship, not quite plane."\n\n→ "The gap between maritime and aviation — that's where the design problem lived. And where Bob Dylan's body knew things the interface didn't."

slides.title: SELF-CHECKOUT
beats: "Self"-checkout is a misnomer.
The chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees.
Age verification. Municipal regulation. Produce indexing.
And the machine — sensor-driven, impatient.
slides.note:
→ "Self-checkout is the everyday version of the same table."

→ "The grocery chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees. Age verification. Municipal regulation. Produce vendors. And the machine itself, ever-ready to flag an unexpected item in the bagging area."

→ "What looks frictionless is a dense web of actors with motives, limits and influence."

⏱ OPTIONAL — cut first if the clock is tight. Regent carries this beat alone.

slides.text: For whose interests does the interface serve?
slides.note:
→ "To design responsibly is to name those actors, question their power, and decide how — and whether — they belong at the table."

→ "It's one thing to design a beautiful interface in your tool of choice. It's another to negotiate with stakeholders. Both are valid, and both land in the interface — the place where the negotiation gets painted."

beats.label: CYBERNETICS

cue.prompt: The loop runs both ways. That's the whole thesis.

slides.title: THE WORD THAT LEFT EARTH
beats: 1960: Clynes & Kline coin "cyborg" in Astronautics.
Cybernetic + organism. Not metaphor — a NASA engineering answer.
Don't rebuild Earth in space. Modify the body to fit the vehicle.
Keep a human alive somewhere it was never built to survive.
slides.note:
→ "The word itself is younger than you'd think. Manfred Clynes and Nathan Kline coined 'cyborg' in 1960 — a paper called 'Cyborgs and Space' in Astronautics."

→ "Cybernetic plus organism. And it wasn't a metaphor — it was an engineering answer."

→ "The problem was keeping a human body alive somewhere it was never built to survive. Their answer wasn't to rebuild Earth-like chambers in space — it was to modify the human to integrate into the vehicle's own loops."

· My Signal+Static piece on this is 'Cyborg — the word that left Earth.'

slides.text: …functioning as an integrated homeostatic system unconsciously.
slides.note:
→ "Here's their actual definition — and I want one word from it."

→ "'For the exogenously extended organizational complex functioning as an integrated homeostatic system unconsciously, we propose the term cyborg.'"

→ "Unconsciously. If you keep noticing your prosthesis, integration has failed."

→ "That's Spiekermann's 'disappears into use.' That's the curb cut going invisible. Same idea, thirty years apart."

slides.alt: 1964 Miami News cyborg diagram showing mechanical human modifications
slides.note: → "This is how their idea traveled — from 1960 engineering paper to 1964 popular imagination."\n\n→ "Camera eyes, tape recorder ears, battery pack, gravity boots. All those mechanical parts that would need to disappear into unconscious use."

slides.text: The world shapes what you make. What you make becomes the world.
slides.note:
→ "Here's the title, and it's the definition of cybernetics: feedback, both directions."

→ "Spiekermann shaped the city, and the institution shaped him back. Berkeley was reshaped, and it reshaped everyone's mobility. The pilot's body reshaped a cockpit that gets inherited by whatever flies next."

→ "The world we move through shapes what we make — and what we make becomes the world someone else moves through."

→ "That two-way arrow is the whole talk."

· Optional, if the room is with me — Maeda at SXSW: 'Feedback is the key to cybernetics, which is the key to the AI era.' Autopilot, lane-assist, agent autoapprovals — same architecture.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 4 min · this is where the thesis stops being illustrated and gets STATED · name the title out loud on the third slide

⚑ 'Cyborgs and Space,' Astronautics, September 1960 — verified · quote the definition exactly, the word is 'unconsciously'

beats.label: TURING

cue.prompt: The test wasn't crossed. It dissolved.

slides.text: For seventy years, this was the finish line.
slides.note:
→ "1950, Alan Turing. If you can't tell — through text-only conversation — whether you're talking to a human or a machine, the machine can reasonably be said to think."

→ "For about seventy years, that faceless conversation was treated as the finish line for machine intelligence."

⚑ Cite 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' 1950 — say the title if anyone's taking notes.

slides.text: Nobody runs the test anymore.
slides.note:
→ "Here's the turn: the veil wasn't crossed. It dissolved."

→ "Nobody runs a formal Turing test anymore. Ambiguity about human-versus-machine is now the default condition of any text you read."

→ "The frame that defined computation for decades just quietly disappeared."

→ "That's the title again, at the level of computation itself: the world — the Turing frame — shaped what got built, and then that world was gone."

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 3 min · setup then dissolution · this restates the title at the level of computation, it is NOT a tangent

⚑ Turing 1950, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — cite properly

beats.label: RESOLUTION

cue.prompt: The question isn't can-you-tell. It's who's accountable.

slides.text: Not "can you tell." Who's accountable.
slides.note:
→ "Once you can't tell anymore, 'can you tell' stops being the interesting question."

→ "The interesting question becomes: who's accountable? Who's responsible for what gets said, decided, or made, when authorship itself can't be resolved?"

· This is why Regent mattered — that was the table. This is where we cash it.

slides.text: Language was never pure individual authorship.
slides.note:
→ "Did you invent the words, did you design the glyphs — no, you never did. And that was always fine."

→ "Because language was never pure individual authorship. It was legible collaboration across a system built by thousands of hands before you arrived."

→ "AI didn't break that. It just made it impossible to keep pretending otherwise."

→ "I've used the word cyborg to describe your practice for forty minutes. That word is the intervention — language is cyborg technology, it changes how you think while you're using it."

→ "Steward maintains and oversees. Curator arranges stuff and context. Negotiator works the table."

→ "These are roles to borrow. 'User' fuses the person and the tool — what's a user without something to use?"

slides.text: Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be.
slides.note:
→ "Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be. It isn't prescriptive — it's diagnostic. It reveals the negotiation table you're already sitting at."

→ "You're all sailing some ship, some assemblage. That's what makes you cyborgs."

→ "So — what's the negotiation table you're sitting at, in your own work? That's where the panel starts."

⏱ Leave the question up. Hand to the panel.

slides.text: RIPTA is moving the bus hub out of Kennedy Plaza. Who was at that table?
slides.note:
→ "RIPTA's board voted in August to move the bus hub from Kennedy Plaza to the train station. Riders organized against it. The Kennedy Plaza Resilience Coalition has been fighting it since 2021."
